name: B7-33
lead: B7-33 is a laboratory-designed, single-chain peptide derived from the B-chain of human relaxin-2, a pleiotropic hormone with vasodilatory and anti-fibrotic properties. It was engineered as a simpler and cheaper mimic of recombinant relaxin-2 (serelaxin), which is costly and laborious to produce [1][2].

B7-33 acts on the relaxin receptor RXFP1 but is described as a functionally selective agonist: it engages some of the receptor's signalling pathways (notably ERK1/2 phosphorylation) while only weakly stimulating others such as cAMP [1][4]. Published work on it consists of cell, mouse and rat studies of vascular function, cardiac remodelling and fibrosis [2][4][5]. It is not an approved medicine, and no human clinical trial has been published.

B7-33 appears in peptide-vendor catalogues in the recovery and tissue-repair category. Its possible link to appearance is through tissue repair: scarring and fibrosis, the build-up of collagen-rich tissue after injury, are among the processes relaxin-pathway research examines, and implant-coating work has used B7-33 to limit fibrous capsules around devices. [7][13] The animal work has been in heart, kidney and implant models rather than skin or cosmetic settings.

paras: Relaxin is a peptide hormone of the insulin superfamily, first described in 1926 by Frederick Hisaw. In pregnancy it is linked to softening of the cervix and loosening of pelvic ligaments, and in animal models it has been reported to reduce collagen secretion by fibroblasts and to stimulate matrix metalloproteinases that break down collagen. [14] Human relaxin-2 acts through the receptor RXFP1, which is found in the heart, smooth muscle, connective tissue and parts of the nervous system. [14]

A recombinant version of human relaxin-2, serelaxin, was developed by Novartis for acute heart failure. Its phase III RELAX-AHF trial reported improvement in breathlessness and reduced worsening of heart failure symptoms, and the FDA granted it breakthrough therapy designation in 2013. On 22 March 2017 Novartis announced that its subsequent global phase III programme did not meet its primary endpoints. Serelaxin is marketed in Russia as Reasanz. [15] Because the two-chain, three-disulfide-bond hormone is laborious and costly to produce, researchers designed single-chain derivatives such as B7-33. [1][2][6]

Human relaxin-2 signals through RXFP1, a G protein-coupled receptor, activating several pathways including cAMP and MAP-kinase signalling [1]. A 2016 chemical-biology study reported that B7-33, a single-chain peptide based on the relaxin B-chain, is a functionally selective RXFP1 agonist that preferentially activates ERK1/2 phosphorylation over cAMP accumulation [1]. Later work on myocardial infarction in mice described the same pathway bias [4].

Medicinal-chemistry papers have continued to modify the peptide, for example with lipidation to improve stability in serum without altering activity, and in the search for a minimal potent relaxin-2 derivative [8][10]. A review covers single-chain peptide agonists of the relaxin receptors more broadly [6].

No studies found in humans. Published research is preclinical: a rodent study reported that B7-33 reproduced vasoprotective effects of serelaxin [2]; a mouse myocardial-infarction study reported attenuated adverse cardiac remodelling [4]; a rat cardiomyopathy model reported more rapid reduction of left-ventricular fibrosis than the ACE inhibitor perindopril [5]; a mouse study examined central relaxin-receptor activation and inflammatory pain [9]; and implant coatings releasing B7-33 were reported to reduce fibrotic encapsulation [7]. A renal-fibrosis imaging method has also been used to assess B7-33 and other anti-fibrotic agents [3].

B7-33 is described in research literature rather than in clinical practice and has no approved indication anywhere. It is offered by research-chemical vendors under recovery-peptide headings. The parent drug, serelaxin, completed large human trials in heart failure, but B7-33 itself has not entered published human trials.

Beyond cardiac and vascular work, B7-33 has been used as the active peptide in several delivery and materials studies. PLGA polymer coatings that release it were reported to reduce fibrotic encapsulation around implants, and it has been loaded onto engineered nanovesicles aimed at fibrosis around tumours in a 2025 cancer model study. [7][11] A 2025 study reported nanoparticle conjugates of anti-fibrotic peptides with activity after oral administration in experimental settings. [12] Chemistry groups continue to modify the peptide to improve stability and potency. [8][10]

card.summary: A lab-made relaxin mimic studied in animals for fibrosis; no human trials and no documented appearance use.
card.note: Preclinical only; no human safety or efficacy data.

quick.overview:
B7-33 is a short peptide designed to imitate part of the hormone relaxin-2, which has anti-fibrotic and blood-vessel-relaxing effects. It was built because the natural hormone is expensive to make.

All published findings are from cells, mice and rats, mainly on heart and kidney fibrosis. No human trial exists, and no source reviewed describes appearance-related use.
quick.mechanism: It binds the relaxin receptor RXFP1 but is biased, activating ERK1/2 signalling more than cAMP, according to the research that characterised it.
quick.risks: Human safety is unstudied. It is not an approved drug anywhere; availability is limited to research-chemical channels.

angle.text: Vendors place B7-33 in the recovery and tissue-repair category, and the research interest is its anti-fibrotic signalling. How that might translate to scars, skin or other visible tissue has not been tested in published work.
